title: On compact formulations for integer programs solved by column generation
contribution: Proves by construction that any integer program solved by column generation has an equivalent compact formulation (block-diagonal, identical subproblems, one column each), so that branching and cutting can work on original variables without breaking the pricing oracle (read in the TU Berlin report version 2003/25).
problem_entry: Branching rules that do not fit the pricing oracle in branch-and-price; in applications often only an extensive formulation and an oracle are given, with no compact model (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Reverse Dantzig-Wolfe: κ copies of the oracle domain give a compact model whose decomposition returns the extensive one; branch by bisecting one copy's domain box, so the oracle keeps its form at every depth (pp. 6-9).
assumptions: Pure IP with general integer columns, no convexity row, finite column set without duplicates; oracle domain closed and bounded in a box; κ known; cost may be non-linear; assumptions called mild, not tested; cutting stock and VRP/crew scheduling as structures (pp. 2-4, 6-7, 9-11).
proof_devices: three-variable, one-row counterexample: under the minimum reduced cost rule one column is never generated, though it forms the unique integer optimum (p. 5)
Proposition 1 by equivalence classes of equal column images with one representative each (pp. 7-8)
Proposition 2 by aggregation and an explicit split of an integer solution into κ unit parts; LP solution divided by κ (pp. 8-9)
branching by bisection of a copy's domain box, three cases including a non-linear cost (p. 9)
identical copies kept aggregated in one oracle until branching makes them differ (p. 9)
experiments: none: no implementation or runs; the applications rebuild compact models of known problems only (pp. 10-11)
positioning: Generalises Desrosiers, Soumis and Desrochers (1984) and the multicommodity framework of Desaulniers et al. (1998); earlier branching rules placed on one rule-versus-oracle trade-off; the weak cutting-stock model attributed to Kantorovich (1960), later corrected (pp. 5-6, 10-11; 05-peer-critique.md §6).
writing: Short, with an English and French abstract; modest register (a straightforward but useful complement; an extremely simple, twenty-year-old approach); an extension labelled as belief (pp. 2-3, 5, 11).
limits_future: Disaggregated master κ times larger; compact model not unique; two formulations to administer; no implementation or test; future: branching adapted to the oracle and the linking constraints, in branch-and-cut, and symmetry reduction (pp. 3, 9, 11).

method_links.note: Step 6: original variables are the natural basis for branching and cutting, and a compact formulation exists under mild assumptions; the applications' cuts are on compact flow variables.
Steps 1-2: the compact model is recovered after the extensive one as a branching device; it is not written first and not run as a benchmark.
Step 6: the Kantorovich attribution here is the one the 2026 book corrected (05-peer-critique.md §6).

title: Solutions to real-world instances of PSPACE-complete stacking
contribution: Shows that a general slab-stacking problem from steel production is PSPACE-complete, yet solves all 18 real instances fast with a guided state-space search and certifies each within 5/4 of optimal by lower bounds from a relaxed MIP.
problem_entry: Industrial slab storage with PSI-BT; the heuristic literature simplifies precedences and has no exact approach; how to get provably good solutions fast for a PSPACE-complete problem (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Hardness (PSPACE-complete; NP-hard without restacking), a greedy valuation-guided search of the state graph counting weighted false positions, and per-instance bounds from a relaxation that keeps the time windows but drops stacks and conflicts (pp. 4-10).
assumptions: Not a MILP; MIP only as the bound model; one item per input at a time, transport times for feasibility only, feasible start; 4 hot-buffer and 14 cold-buffer PSI-BT instances; the MIP bound needs incoming items, so it does not apply to the cold buffer (pp. 3-4, 9-11).
proof_devices: PSPACE membership by Savitch's theorem (p. 4)
PSPACE-completeness by reduction from nondeterministic constraint logic with and/or gadgets of two buffer stacks (pp. 4-5)
NP-hardness without restacking for heights of at least six, from mutual exclusion scheduling on permutation graphs (p. 6)
ingredients of the first proof named and removed in a second hardness theorem (p. 6)
Towers of Hanoi valuation makes the greedy search reproduce the unique optimal sequence (pp. 7-8)
relaxation MIP (as many stacks as items, no conflicts, maximise direct moves) solved with CPLEX 10.1 as certificate; LP bound for v3 (pp. 9-10)
experiments: Standard Linux PC, CPLEX 10.1, no time limit, no baseline run; greedy gaps 4.9-11.6% hot and 13.5-24.8% cold, rollout better at over 1,000 times the run time; Table 1 gap is (UB-LB)/UB, Table 2 gap (UB-LB)/LB (my computation); 5/4 holds on all 18 instances (largest ratio 1.248); promised lookahead results absent (pp. 9-11).
positioning: Against simplifying heuristics (simulated annealing, simulation, genetic algorithms, state-space evaluation); links to the Towers of Hanoi, sliding-block puzzles and stack sorting; cost-to-go and rollout from Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis (pp. 2-3, 6, 9).
writing: Abstract runs hardness, speed, guarantee, hedged firstness; the discussion pre-empts the objection that 25% is weak with three comments, one an approximation-factor analogy that sets a-posteriori gaps beside a-priori guarantees (pp. 1, 11-12).
limits_future: Bounds miss restacking; restacking complexity not characterised even for two stacks; no data on manual operation; future: hardness by restacking complexity, discrete optimisation for PSPACE-complete problems (pp. 11-12).

method_links.note: Headline claim sized to measured per-instance bounds (5/4 holds on all 18 instances, my computation); failed rollout reported with its cost; Taste G1 and H2: a certified prototype at two plants.
No baseline run (step 3); two different, undefined gap measures and a missing lookahead analysis (step 5); the approximation analogy stretches the claim (step 6).
The full MIP is declared intractable without a run; MIP serves as a certificate on a relaxation, not as a competitor.

title: Optimizing the cargo express service of Swiss Federal Railways
contribution: Models the tactical planning of SBB Cargo Express three ways (compact ILP, hierarchical branch-and-cut decomposition, integrated set-partitioning model by column generation) and shows on one real instance that the integrated model saves 7,410 cost units, about a fifth, over the hierarchical one.
problem_entry: A real two-hub overnight freight service planned by hand; existing freight-rail models lack detailed schedules or violate hard load and time-window limits (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: A ladder of three models of increasing detail; the integrated Model 2 prices scheduled routes by shipment-elementary labeling and finds integer plans by dive-and-generate (pp. 2-7, 10-13).
assumptions: MHSOP, strongly NP-hard; 15-minute slots; one averaged instance of 200 shipments on a network condensed to 121 nodes, time windows built from the current plan plus one hour, realistic parameters; covering instead of partitioning (pp. 4, 6, 10, 13-14).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: routing problem transformed into a DCVRP with K extra nodes, proof in an ETH report (pp. 7-8)
distance cuts separated heuristically, first locally, then globally valid via 1-tree and assignment bounds (pp. 8-9)
simplified scheduling variant equivalent to an NP-hard linear-arrangement problem, solved by a time-indexed ILP (pp. 9-10)
constraint redundancy: any two of three families imply the third (p. 7)
master seeded with one direct-engine column per shipment for feasibility (p. 10)
shipment-elementary labeling with partial elementarity, fractional-knapsack completion bound and time-slot dominance (pp. 11-12)
heuristic pricing, perturbation, column aging; stabilisation that did not pay off (p. 12)
dive-and-generate with Phase-I repair and local improvement (pp. 12-13)
experiments: 3 GHz Linux PC, 4 GB, CPLEX 9, SYMPHONY 5, SCIP; one real instance plus a toy; Model 0 found nothing feasible in 7 h on the toy; Model 1 cost 42,686, its routing runs taking about 10 days, with a hub overload; Model 2 35,276 after 85 h, root value 29,217 at tailing-off with its bound status unstated; the loss of 7,410 is 21.0% of Model 2's cost (paper: 20%) (pp. 10, 13-15).
positioning: Freight-rail surveys and blocking or routing models judged unfit (no load limits, yard capacities or schedules); Gorman's tabu search violates hard constraints; hedged firstness for integrating all tactical steps (pp. 1-2).
writing: A three-way comparison promised, two paragraphs delivered; a strong conclusion (consistently, provably good) on one instance; limits listed concretely; a closing hope for out-of-the-box solvers (pp. 2, 14-15).
limits_future: Days of computing, an overload in Model 1, one averaged instance, no comparison with the current plan, branching hardly tested, drivers, switchbacks and furcations not modelled; future: these in pricing, and branching rules (pp. 14-15).

method_links.note: Compact model written and run first, for partner feedback and the optimisation potential; its toy failure motivated the decomposition; Model 2 built on SCIP and Model 1 on SYMPHONY; pricing is a dedicated labeling algorithm.
The compact model ran only on an 11-shipment toy, never on the 200-shipment instance, and no bounds were compared.

title: The concept of recoverable robustness, linear programming recovery, and railway applications
contribution: Introduces recoverable robustness, plans paired with limited recovery algorithms, and shows that with LP recovery and small right-hand-side scenario sets the robust problem is a polynomial-size LP, or an unchanged integer model plus a linear block, with railway timetabling and platforming as applications.
problem_entry: Railway practice uses slack plus limited recovery, but plan, slack and recovery are not optimised together; stochastic programs are too large and strict robustness is over-conservative for timetabling (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: A precaution is a plan plus an admissible recovery algorithm, with strict robustness as a special case; LP recovery is dualised, worst cases sit at unit vectors of the l1 ball, giving a compact LP; integer plans get a linear block via row slacks (pp. 4-5, 16-21).
assumptions: LP, ILP or MILP with right-hand-side uncertainty in S_1 or S_k, k very small; recovery must be an LP; small disturbances bounded by Δ on at most k arcs; full scenario knowledge at recovery, called a fundamental weakness (pp. 9, 13, 18-20).
proof_devices: strong LP duality of the inner recovery problem (equation (28), p. 19)
maximum over the l1 ball at Δ times a unit vector, giving one recovery copy per row (pp. 19-20)
Theorem 1 and Corollaries 1-2 for S_k with one copy per k-subset, proof sketched by analogy (p. 20)
scenario expansion versus a three-player game with the same feasible plans (pp. 17-18)
row slacks as the link between the original ILP and the robustness LP (p. 21)
cited PSPACE-hardness of multistage delay management motivates rule-based recovery (pp. 13-14)
experiments: None run here; a cited study (Caprara, Galli, Stiller, Toth 2008) at Palermo Centrale cuts the maximum propagated delay by 14.29-35.03% at equal throughput, while CPU time rises 2.6 to 547 times (my computation), which the text does not discuss; no hardware or solver data (pp. 24-26).
positioning: Against two-stage stochastic programming and classical robust optimisation (Soyster), the latter recast as strict robustness; timetabling previously treated only by stochastic programming; ARRIVAL work listed without comparison (pp. 1-3, 5, 9).
writing: Framework in three named steps; strong framing (robust timetabling makes sense only as recovery robust) beside honest scoping (theorems cover only strong specialisations; very small k); the conclusion summarises and names no future work (pp. 3-4, 7-8, 12, 20, 26).
limits_future: Very small k, no integer recovery, scenario expansions too large, the online weakness, myopic waiting rules; time cost unstated; matrix disturbances left to Stiller's thesis; no future work stated (pp. 3, 12-13, 15, 20, 26).

method_links.note: Step 6 in the theory: the general concept is scoped explicitly, and the S_k result is limited to very small k.

title: Experiments with a generic Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition for integer programs
contribution: Turns SCIP into a generic branch-price-and-cut solver (GCG 0.7) that decomposes a MIP by a user-supplied block structure and runs the original and extended problems as two synchronized SCIP instances, beating plain SCIP on capacitated p-median, bin packing and a temporal knapsack forced into blocks.
problem_entry: Branch-and-cut is generic, branch-and-price ad hoc; even generic decomposition codes rebuild preprocessing and tree management; the goal is stated as a future solver's log (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Two synchronized SCIP instances: the original coordinates the search, and the extended master is solved by column generation inside a relaxation handler; all SCIP components are inherited; branching and cuts on original variables (pp. 4-8).
assumptions: MIPs with linking rows and a (bordered) block-diagonal part, bounded blocks, discretisation for pure integer blocks; structure from a user file; p-median, 540 bin-packing instances, 70 temporal-knapsack instances forced into 32- or 64-row blocks (pp. 3-4, 9-11).
proof_devices: invariant: corresponding nodes pruned together, since they share dual and primal bounds (p. 5)
Lagrangean bound when all pricing problems are solved to optimality; early termination for integral objectives (p. 6)
branching enforced in pricing, with propagation fixing incompatible columns to zero (p. 7)
only basis-free cuts (knapsack cover, MIR, flow cover), no Gomory cuts (pp. 7-8)
aggregation of identical blocks (p. 7)
black-box pricing solvers with Farkas pricing (p. 6)
experiments: GCG 0.7, SCIP 1.2.0.5, CPLEX 12.1 as LP solver; two Core2 Quad machines; shifted geometric means (shift 10 for time and nodes, 100 for gaps); plain SCIP the only baseline; p-median 220.1 vs 294.0 s, knapsack pricer -61.7%; all 540 bin-packing instances (about 42 min by the table; text: under 90); temporal knapsack 56 vs 5 of 70 solved, 3.8-4.1 times faster; text-table slips (21 vs 32.2 nodes; 8% vs 2.8% total time) and undiscussed losses on new4 1-3 (my reading) (pp. 8-13).
positioning: Among frameworks (ABACUS, BCP, MINTO) and generic decomposition codes (BaPCod, DIP, G12; only DIP public); credits Vanderbeck; complements a maintained solver instead of starting from scratch; expects tailored codes to win (pp. 2-3, 8).
writing: Framed as experiments, opening with Situation; vision hedged by scepticism, then a months-not-years forecast; summary sized (first experiments, very promising for structured problems) with an open question on unknown structure (pp. 1-2, 13).
limits_future: Structure must be supplied, heuristics cannot run on the original, no stabilisation, column pool or Gomory basis, tailored codes faster; future: a SCIP release and detecting whether and how to decompose (pp. 4, 8, 13).

method_links.note: Steps 2, 4, 5, 6: plain SCIP on the original model as baseline; structure supplied by the user; built on a framework that manages the tree; branching and cuts on original variables.
Step 2: the yardstick is the host framework SCIP, not the strongest MILP solver; CPLEX 12.1 only as LP solver.

No competitor or tailored code re-run; two text-table mismatches, an undiscussed loss on three easy instances, a bin-packing comparison without SCIP numbers.
A two-point option space (32 vs 64 rows per block) measured, not argued; the full enumeration of reformulations came with SEA 2018.
